title: Duplication of specialized cis-acting elements SLI and SLIII in the viral RNA 3'UTR enables mosquito-borne orthoflavivirus adaptation to avian hosts.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the full Europe PMC supplement (2.48 MB): it is 20 figure images plus one 17-page PDF. I extracted the PDF text and read every table: Table S1 = PCR primer sequences, Table S2 = 16 single-base changes in the viral 3'UTR (untranslated region) after passaging, Table S3 = ~100 proteins pulled down with viral RNA (UniProt accession, ratio, p-value). I grepped the complete open-access full text (181,843 characters) for any repository accession (ProteomeXchange/PRIDE/iProX, GEO, SRA, BioProject, Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad): zero hits. Europe PMC text-mining and the NCBI link search returned only 11 pre-existing GenBank accessions for virus strains other labs already deposited, plus one DOI.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All quantitative results (luciferase replicon curves, virus titres in duck/mammalian/mosquito cells, duckling and mouse virulence, CELF2 binding experiments) are described in the text and plotted in figure images only; I could not open any numeric file behind them. The claim that the mass-spectrometry experiment was done at all rests on the methods section, since no raw or processed proteomics file is deposited anywhere.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL, verified. The data availability statement reads 'The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation' - i.e. on request, which the rubric treats as a failure. I confirmed by opening the supplement and searching the whole text that nothing is deposited: no ProteomeXchange/PRIDE, GEO, SRA, BioProject, Zenodo, Figshare or Dryad identifier exists. The only machine-readable numbers are two small tables locked inside a PDF.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, verified. There is no label column anywhere. Any target (replication efficiency of a 3'UTR mutant, or host-cell preference) would have to be read off figure panels by hand, which is construction by inference, not a column.

a3_inputs_present.note: Partially true but irrelevant given A1/A2: the mutant 3'UTR sequences could be rebuilt from GenBank strain records plus the primer table, but they are not supplied as sequences.

a4_units_stated.note: The two PDF tables do label their columns (base position, reference/alternate base, variant type, cell line; UniProt accession, abundance ratio, p-value), so units are not the problem here.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, verified. Largest usable tables are Table S2 with 16 rows (single-base changes after passaging) and Table S3 with roughly 100 rows (proteins enriched on viral RNA). The experimental unit the paper actually studies is the engineered virus mutant, of which there are on the order of 20. All are far under the ~1,500-row (or ~400 for classification) bar.

a6_fits_laptop.note: The entire supplement is 2.48 MB. Size was never the issue.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The table contents I extracted match their captions; there is simply almost nothing to count.

a8_label_provenance.note: Where measurements exist they are genuine wet-lab readouts (luciferase, plaque titres, animal survival, mass-spectrometry ratios), not another model's output. This killer is not what sinks the paper.

existing_models.name: RNAVirHost (2024, machine-learning predictor of the host of an RNA virus from its genome)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not assessed in detail - the evaluation stopped at Part A, so I did not verify its reported numbers or split.

existing_models.name: Codon-usage / unsupervised host-identification algorithm for flaviviruses (Life, 2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not assessed; retrieved by search only to establish that virus-host prediction from sequence is an active area.

backbone.name: RNA-FM or a nucleotide language model would in principle suit viral 3'UTR sequences
backbone.hardware: CPU would suffice for ~20 short sequences, but there is nothing to train on

integration.join_key: GenBank accession and NCBI taxonomy identifier
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could a model read a mosquito-borne flavivirus 3'UTR and say which vertebrate host it is adapted to? - a real question, but this paper supplies mechanism, not the labelled sequence table that would answer it.

controls.positive_control: None available: with ~20 engineered mutants there is no train/test structure to control.
controls.negative_control: Not applicable - no model can be trained.
controls.external_validation: GenBank flavivirus 3'UTRs with known host association would be the external set, but it would have to be the primary dataset, not a validation of this paper.

honest_claim_h3: No honest model claim can be made from this paper's data: nothing is deposited, and the largest machine-readable table has 16 rows.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a virus's 3' untranslated region sequence to predict which animal host the virus replicates best in.
plain_idea.train_on: Would need the sequence of the structured region at the end of the viral genome for each virus strain, with a few hundred to a few thousand strains. This paper provides roughly 20 engineered mutants, and none as a downloadable sequence file.
plain_idea.predict: How well the virus replicates in bird cells versus mammal cells versus mosquito cells. The truth would come from luciferase replicon readings and virus titre assays - which this paper performed but published only as figure plots.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Veterinary and public-health surveillance groups would like to flag, from sequence alone, when a mosquito-borne flavivirus is shifting towards birds or poultry. Even a failed model would tell us whether these stem-loop duplications carry enough signal on their own.

ml_idea: The only idea the paper suggests - predict avian versus mammalian host adaptation from the flavivirus 3' untranslated region sequence - would have to be built almost entirely from public GenBank sequences plus host-of-isolation metadata, with this paper contributing only mechanistic context and about 20 hand-made mutants. That is a different project that happens to cite this paper, not a project based on its data.

effort.compute_note: Only the 2.48 MB supplement was handled; no modelling workload exists to estimate, so timing fields are null rather than guessed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the data availability statement, then unzip the supplement and count the rows in its largest table. Both took under five minutes and both killed it: 'available from the authors on request' and 16 rows.

verdict_reason: Classic wet-lab virology paper with no deposited data. Verified in the files: the supplement is figures plus one PDF whose biggest tables hold 16 variant rows and ~100 pulldown proteins, the data availability statement is 'on request', and no repository accession for new data exists anywhere in the text. Fails A1, A2 and A5.
